William Strong
WIL-yum STRONG
n. proper (Westminster Divine and Puritan typologist; c.1611–1654)
William, from Germanic Wilhelmus (will-helmet; from wil, will, desire, + helm, helmet, protection); Strong is an Old English surname from the adjective strang (powerful, vigorous). William Strong was among the most creative exegetes of the Westminster generation, celebrated especially for his typological exposition of the Mosaic sacrificial system as pointing toward Christ.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

William Strong (c.1611–1654) was a Westminster Divine and Congregationalist minister celebrated for his profound command of biblical typology — the interpretive method that reads Old Testament institutions, persons, and events as divinely ordered foreshadowings of Christ and the gospel. He served as minister at St Dunstan's in the West, London, and was among the ablest expositors of the sacrificial system of Leviticus and Numbers in his generation. His great work, A Discourse of the Two Covenants (published posthumously, 1678), stands among the finest covenant-theology expositions of the era, tracing the relationship between the covenant of works and the covenant of grace through the whole of Scripture with an architectonic clarity that few of his contemporaries matched. Strong understood typology not as allegorical fancy but as the literary and theological structure God embedded in the Mosaic economy: every priest, every sacrifice, every feast pointed toward the One High Priest whose one sacrifice fulfilled and displaced them all. Hebrews was his primary New Testament interpreter of this structure: “the Law, since it has only a shadow of the good things to come” (Heb 10:1), existed not as an end in itself but as the God-ordained shadow whose substance is Christ. His death in 1654 cut short a career that had already placed him among the first rank of Reformed biblical theologians; the posthumous publication of his covenant theology treatise ensured his influence extended into the next generation. Matthew Poole drew on him; the covenant-theology tradition that ran from Ball to Owen and Flavel to Boston is unintelligible without Strong's typological-covenantal synthesis.

Webster 1828 Definition

Westminster Divine and minister at St Dunstan's in the West whose mastery of biblical typology and covenant theology, expressed in A Discourse of the Two Covenants (1678), made him among the finest Puritan expositors of the Mosaic economy's Christological design.

STRONG, William (c.1611–1654). Westminster Divine, Congregationalist minister, and Puritan biblical theologian; minister of St Dunstan's in the West, London. His literary legacy rests primarily on A Discourse of the Two Covenants (1678), published posthumously by his congregation, which synthesized covenant theology and biblical typology with unusual architectural clarity.

Strong was a member of the Westminster Assembly (1643–1649) and signed the Solemn League and Covenant, though his ecclesiology was Congregationalist rather than Presbyterian. His Assembly participation placed him in the generation that produced both the Westminster Confession and the Savoy Declaration, and his work bears the marks of both traditions’ covenantal thinking.

His typological method was rooted in Hebrews: the Levitical system was not a human achievement or a bare pedagogical structure but the God-inscribed shadow of Christ’s high-priestly work. Strong read Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers with a Christological precision that connected the tabernacle furniture, the priestly garments, the daily and annual sacrifices, and the great feasts to the gospel's substance in Christ.

The Discourse of the Two Covenants distinguishes the covenant of works (made with Adam in innocency) from the covenant of grace (made with the elect in Christ from before the foundation of the world) and traces the covenant of grace through its various administrations — Adamic promise, Abrahamic oath, Mosaic shadow, Davidic confirmation, and new covenant fulfillment — without confusing the unity of the one covenant of grace with the diversity of its historical forms.

His early death at approximately forty-three means that his influence operated primarily through the posthumous edition and through his Assembly colleagues who knew his work firsthand; the Reformed and Congregationalist covenant-theology tradition that became normative through John Owen, Thomas Goodwin, and their successors was shaped in part by Strong's careful distinctions.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 10:1 — "For the Law, since it has only a shadow of the good things to come, and not the very form of things — can never, by the same sacrifices year by year, which they offer continually, make perfect those who draw near."

Colossians 2:17 — "things which are a shadow of what is to come; but the substance belongs to Christ."

Hebrews 8:5 — "who serve a copy and shadow of the heavenly things. As Moses was warned by God when he was about to erect the tabernacle: “See,” He says, “that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain.”"

Hebrews 9:11 — "But when Christ appeared as a high priest of the good things to come — He entered through the greater and more perfect tabernacle, not made with hands, that is, not of this creation —"

Modern Corruption

Dispensational literalism diminishes typology by collapsing “fulfillment” into a future earthly restoration of Levitical forms; Strong's covenant-typological method, following Hebrews, insists that the substance having come in Christ, the shadows are fulfilled and displaced, not merely postponed.

expand to see more

Dispensational hermeneutics, from Darby and Scofield through modern dispensationalists, treats the Levitical system and its institutions as waiting for a future fulfillment in a restored temple and a reinstituted priesthood during a millennial reign. This reading makes the shadows eternal in form even after the Substance has appeared. Strong's covenant-typological method follows the New Testament's own hermeneutic, especially Hebrews: the tabernacle was a copy and shadow of heavenly things (Heb 8:5); the law had only a shadow of the good things to come (Heb 10:1); Christ has entered the greater and more perfect tabernacle not made with hands (Heb 9:11). The shadows are not postponed; they are fulfilled and therefore displaced.

Liberal historical-critical approaches read the Mosaic legislation as the product of Ancient Near Eastern priestly tradition, comparative Ugaritic religion, and post-exilic redaction, stripping it of its Christological design. The typological method Strong practiced is incompatible with this approach not because it ignores the historical particularity of the texts but because it refuses to privilege the historical-comparative frame over the canon's own interpretive logic. The New Testament’s reading of the Old is authoritative; the critics' reading is not. Strong would have recognized the historical-critical dismantling of Mosaic typology as an attack on the hermeneutic that makes the Bible the coherent story of one Redeemer.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Formed in the covenant-theology tradition of William Ames, Ball, and the Westminster Assembly; his typological method was anchored in the epistle to the Hebrews and expressed through an architectonic covenant theology that distinguished the one covenant of grace from its diverse historical administrations.

expand to see more

Westminster Assembly (1643–1649) — Strong attended as a Congregationalist member; the Assembly's debates over covenant theology, church government, and worship formed the intellectual environment in which his most mature thought developed.

William Ames and Puritan covenant theology — the trajectory from Perkins through Ames to the Westminster divines established the covenant of works / covenant of grace distinction that Strong's Discourse refined; he is an heir and developer of this tradition, not its originator.

Epistle to the Hebrews as hermeneutical key — Strong read Hebrews as the apostolic interpretation of the Mosaic economy; every typological connection he drew was anchored in the apostolic precedent of Hebrews' sustained argument that Christ is the antitype of the whole Levitical order.

A Discourse of the Two Covenants (1678) — posthumously published; the work that preserved his influence; its distinction between the historical administrations of the one covenant of grace and its clear differentiation of the covenant of works from the covenant of grace became standard Reformed covenantal vocabulary.

Congregationalist polity — like Thomas Goodwin and Philip Nye at the Westminster Assembly, Strong was a leading Congregationalist; his Independency did not separate him from the Reformed confessional tradition but expressed it in a different ecclesiological form.

Usage

"Strong's typological method is the corrective to two errors in reading the Old Testament: the literalist dispensational error that expects the shadows to return, and the liberal error that strips the texts of any Christological design; the apostolic hermeneutic of Hebrews is the standard both err against."

"Studying A Discourse of the Two Covenants alongside Owen's Hebrews commentary and Flavel's typological works gives a comprehensive picture of how the mid-seventeenth-century Puritan tradition read the whole of Scripture as one covenantal story pointing to and fulfilled in Christ."

"His career illustrates that confessional Reformed and Congregationalist believers shared a common exegetical tradition even while disagreeing on church polity — the covenant-typological framework was not Presbyterian but Reformed, and Congregationalists participated in it as fully as any."
